Setting.name: enabled
Setting.label: Enabled
Setting.helpText: Master switch. Turn this off and every host reverts to the levels in its own log4j2.properties on its next sync tick (within ~60 seconds), without any config being lost.

Setting.name: requiredCapability
Setting.label: Required capability
Setting.helpText: Capability the logged-in user (or one of their workgroups) must hold to view or change logger levels. There is no SysAdmin bypass - the check is exactly this capability name. Ships as SystemAdministrator so it works out of the box; point it at a dedicated capability such as LoggerAdmin to grant developers logging control without granting them everything else.

Setting.name: defaultTtlMinutes
Setting.label: Default TTL (minutes)
Setting.helpText: Pre-selected lifetime for a new override. Debug logging that nobody remembers to switch off is the usual way this kind of tool causes an incident, so overrides expire by default.

Setting.name: maxTtlMinutes
Setting.label: Maximum TTL (minutes)
Setting.helpText: Upper bound on how long an override may live. Requests above this are clamped down to it. Set to 0 to allow permanent overrides that never expire (not recommended in production).

Setting.name: allowRootLogger
Setting.label: Allow root logger
Setting.helpText: Whether the root logger may be targeted by a new override. Setting root to DEBUG or TRACE turns on every logger in the JVM at once, which on a busy host can fill a disk in minutes. Off by default; turn it on deliberately and briefly. This is not the only guard: root also ships in Untouchable loggers, which is what stops it being Suppressed or Cleared from the table. To actually raise root you have to turn this on AND take root out of that list.

Setting.name: untouchableLoggers
Setting.label: Untouchable loggers
Setting.helpText: Loggers this plugin refuses to change, comma separated. Their Suppress and Clear controls are greyed out on the Logger Manager page, and the API rejects any attempt to override them, so a protected logger cannot be altered from here at all. A bare name matches that name only - protecting sailpoint does NOT protect sailpoint.api.Provisioner, otherwise the plugin could not do its job. Use * to protect a whole tree deliberately: sailpoint.* covers everything beneath sailpoint but not sailpoint itself, *.Provisioner matches from the other end, and * protects everything. Ships with root and sailpoint: root sets the level for every logger in the JVM at once, and sailpoint is the parent of the whole product, so raising or silencing either affects far more than whoever clicked expects. Note root is guarded twice - Allow root logger decides whether it may be targeted at all, this list decides whether it may be changed or cleared, and both have to allow it. Clear the field to protect nothing.

Setting.name: showLogFiles
Setting.label: Show log files on the page
Setting.helpText: Whether the page can show the end of this host's own log files. Only files that host's log4j2 configuration already writes to can be read - one is picked from that list rather than named by path, so there is nothing to point elsewhere. Reads come from the end of the file, are capped, and are audited. Turn this off if log content is more sensitive than the capability guarding this plugin.

Setting.name: logTailKb
Setting.label: Log tail size (KB)
Setting.helpText: How much of the end of a log file to read at once. Capped at 512 regardless of this value. Larger is slower to render and rarely more useful - filter the text instead.

Setting.name: hostsFromServersOnly
Setting.label: Take the host list from IIQ only
Setting.helpText: Whether IdentityIQ's own Server list is the only source of truth for which hosts exist. On by default: the Host Status table shows exactly the hosts IIQ knows about, so retiring a host in IIQ retires it here too. Each host also writes a status record of its own - what it applied, which log4j2 config it read, what is live in its JVM - and when a host is removed from IIQ that record is left behind. With this on, those orphaned records are kept out of the table and reported above it with a button to clear them, so nothing accumulates unnoticed. Turn it off and the orphaned hosts appear everywhere instead, marked ORPHANED on their chip and dropped by default from every section, so you can still read what they last reported and still aim an override at them - useful when a host was removed from IIQ but you are not certain its JVM is actually down. Nothing there will confirm an override, so those hosts sit on pending.

Setting.name: permanentLoggers
Setting.label: Permanent loggers (never expire)
Setting.helpText: NOT the normal way to turn a logger on. For day-to-day use, open the Logger Manager page (gear icon -> Plugins -> click 'Logger Manager', or go straight to plugins/pluginPage.jsf?pn=TurnOnLoggers) and use the 'Turn on a logger' form there - it has a logger picker, per-host targeting and an expiry. This field is the exception: loggers listed here have NO expiry, so they stay on until you edit this box. Use it only for a logger you want on indefinitely. They still appear in the Logger Manager page's table marked 'from settings', so that page remains a single list of everything that is on. Format: comma-separated logger=LEVEL, with an optional @host suffix to restrict one item to a single host. Example: sailpoint.api.Provisioner=DEBUG, sailpoint.connector=TRACE@iiq-app-02
